note: Supports the time (7:30 am), the unit (8th Illinois Cavalry), the officer (Lt. Marcellus Jones) and the place (western yard of the Wisler house, carbine on a fence post) of the first-shot row; the NPS page calls it the first shot of the battle; the row itself notes the claim is symbolic.
The seminary main building was used for weeks after the battle as a hospital for both sides (the row concerns July 1: this passage dates the use only as lasting weeks).
McPherson farmhouse, bank barn, stables and wagon shed sheltered the wounded on July 1 and stayed filled under Confederate control.
A July 5 visitor found the barn, wagon shed, tenant house, pig sty and barnyard crowded with badly wounded men.
The barn sheltered Union regiments, sharpshooters fired from the stone gable walls, and it served as shelter and hospital after the fighting.
The inventory records the barn as a shelter and hospital after the fighting; no burning is mentioned.
The two large Weikert farm buildings were field hospitals during and after the battle for the casualties at Little Round Top and the Wheatfield Road.
Dr. Brinton was in charge of the 2nd Division, 11th Corps hospital at the George Spangler farm where Armistead was taken.
The 1988 study names the 11th Corps hospital at the George Spangler farm as the site of Armistead's death.
The Spangler farm complex served as the 11th Corps field hospital.
The Spangler farm complex served as the 11th Corps field hospital.
Mary Thompson's property, used as Lee's headquarters, lost fencing and had breastworks built and a garden destroyed.
Col. Aiken recalled two fences lining the Emmitsburg Road; the report records worm fencing on the east boundary of the Rose and Snyder fields documented in the 1868 Warren map.
Worm fencing around the Peach Orchard and Rose North Orchard documented in the 1863 Bachelder map, the 1872 survey and photographs.
The study says a post and rail fence paralleled the Emmitsburg Road and that no stone fence is known there (stones may have been piled under the rails).
The park report says the whole west slope of Little Round Top had been cut clear a year before the battle except for a few scattered trees and light undergrowth.
On the Warren map Big Round Top has a heavy growth of round-leaf trees, oak and pine; Brady photographs show the Little Round Top slope nearly bare.
The inventory says the western side of Little Round Top was open at the time of the battle.

Sworn statement of the tenant John T. Slentz of January 8, 1883 in the landlord's claim file (transcribed in the NPS McPherson farm study, Appendix B): the day before the battle General Buford's command occupied the place until 10 a.m. the next day and cut and threw down about a quarter mile of post and rail fence to make way for the battle (about one cord of the rails was used as fuel). The claim file the earlier note (DD-TL01-04) says was not read has now been read: it is a sworn statement of 1883, a participant's account twenty years after, not a record of 1863; the appraisement of July 22, 1863 counts the rails destroyed on July 1-4 together (NPSX-HS-MCPHERSON-p106-01).

The NPS study's narrative of the same event (the tenant watched Buford's troopers cut and throw down about a quarter mile of post and rail fence, and another cord of rails used for firewood); its basis is the tenant's claims file (footnote 49).

The tenant's petition under the Act of April 9, 1868 (as transcribed in Appendix A of the study) says the farm was occupied by Buford's cavalry, who encamped on it on June 30, 1863, and that on July 1 General Buford directed him to remove his family from the house: supports the presence of Buford's cavalry on the farm on June 30 and the removal of the family on July 1; it does not itself mention the dismantling of fences.
The ambulatory wounded sought refuge in the McPherson farmhouse and barn on July 1 and at dusk the fields were strewn with the dead and wounded of both armies (NPS McPherson farm study).

According to Sarah Slentz, over 200 soldiers were cared for in the house and barn alone until they could be moved to other field hospitals; two soldiers were buried in the garden (an account of about 1930 as told in the NPS study).

A Union lieutenant's account (quoted by the NPS study): on reaching McPherson's barn he found it full of bleeding and mangled soldiers without a surgeon; the barn held the wounded of the first day through the night and after.

A chaplain's account of the day after the armies withdrew (quoted by the NPS study): the barn above and below, the wagon shed, the tenant house, the pig sty and the barnyard crowded with badly wounded soldiers; no surgeon until about noon.

A Virginian's account (quoted by the NPS Pickett's Charge study): on July 3 the board fences along the Emmitsburg Road were still mostly standing when his regiment reached the road; carried as a conflict with the statement that the road fences near Codori's house were nearly destroyed the day before (NPSX-COMMON-PRIDE-1-p131-01).

The study says a fence ran east-west from the Emmitsburg Road to the Angle wall at the slashing along the north boundary of the Codori farm, the only fence between the road and the Union defenses that Garnett's brigade would have crossed (hedged).
